sm: The episode opens with a rapid run of short clips pulled from the conversation to come. The speakers call Grand Theft Auto the cultural phenomenon of 2026, argue over whether the new game is woke or better described as feminized, and describe it as a game about a man who hates himself. One guest says conservative commentators talk down to people who play video games, another says a developer was pushed out after calling himself pro-life, and another says some studios make games that turn off most of their audience. The clips close with a question about the most fun game to play with friends.

Jeremy Boreing opens with the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 the previous Thursday. He says it sold 32.5 million copies before release and took in 3.8 billion dollars on day one, which he calls the largest entertainment launch in history. It holds a Metacritic score of 99, and he mentions a survey estimating a million and a half Americans called in sick to play. He notes it came thirteen years after the last entry, and describes the odd detail that the in-game girlfriend wants chores done around the house. He adds that the average American boy spends over two hours a day on games.

Boreing then frames the industry's recent history. For about fifteen years, he says, studios treated their players with contempt and hired consultants to make stories sufficiently woke, citing Dragon Age The Veilguard, which EA said came in about fifty percent below expectations before BioWare was shut down. He says around 57,000 industry jobs have been lost since 2022. He asks whether GTA 6 is good culture, whether it is a win for conservatives, and whether it is art or arrested development. He introduces John Gibson, a game studio founder forced out of his company over his pro-life views, and Greg Owen, a pop culture critic.

Boreing asks Gibson why the game is so popular. Gibson says it started with the fantasy of causing havoc without consequences, and recalls that the original game became a hit when a bug made police crash into the player's cars. Over time it grew into an everything simulator. Boreing says it works as a nostalgic, satirical and subversive cultural artifact for millennials, and compares it to West Coast gangster rap, which both celebrates and comments on the world that creates its subject. Owen recalls his mother refusing to buy San Andreas, and says the real draw is a communal experience and fear of missing out, with multiplayer still to come.

The group discusses why violent games may show little link to real violence. Owen says games are systems, and boys like testing systems, taking apart a bike just to see inside it, so players try to break the game or find developer secrets. Gibson adds that with every frontier explored, open world games give men a place to explore and conquer. Boreing replies that this does not explain four billion dollars in a week, and says the naughty, rated R content is intrinsic to the appeal. Gibson and Owen add the long buildup, a fight over games as a battleground to browbeat boys, and young men who feel hopeless and want a fantasy they can share with friends.

Boreing describes two political camps on games. He says the left tolerates gaming but objects to the content men want, such as attractive women, and prefers girl bosses and androgynous characters. Many conservatives, he says, see gaming past age thirteen as arrested development, with conservative women commentators comparing it to pornography and drug use and calling it unattractive. He points out that the game itself satirizes this, with a girlfriend who withholds affection unless chores are done. Men, he says, reject both extremes, and playing games is simply what men do with weekend leisure, as golf and beer once were.

Owen says most gamers do not think they are making a political statement and resent being told that their hobby is one. Boreing cites studies that games help problem solving and a survey in which about the same share of gamers and non-gamers call themselves failures, while far more pornography users do. The guests agree any hobby can be abused, from football to gambling, but that people want escape from stressful lives. Boreing adds that women have their own escapism and that men and women tend to err in different directions. He argues that lecturing men makes them less likely to step up and be responsible.

Boreing says he is five hours in and finds the first chapter a slog, noting that critics give the game 99 while user scores are far lower. Gibson says the early hours feel like a Sweet Baby Inc. era product, with mundane tasks such as drinking water and a warning system that punishes bad behavior in a game about crime. Boreing counters that the game satirizes its characters, noting that reportedly most of the thirteen endings go badly for the male lead. Owen notes that one character is a girl boss while the other mumbles, though he says players report the relationship is more balanced in the second chapter, that the game pokes fun at liberals, and that he has not finished it.

Boreing observes that the game was made by Scottish developers, so American terms like woke may not fit, and compares it to Christopher Nolan's Odyssey, which he finds distracting in casting but not truly woke. Gibson clarifies that it is not peak woke but carries a whiff of 2023. He points to protected classes, saying you can shoot up a church but not a gay bar, and that prostitutes are gone. Owen prefers calling it feminized rather than woke, defining woke as identity-based morality. He says the lead writer Dan Houser left Rockstar, leaving a relational story where the player lacks agency, unlike Red Dead Redemption 2, which he calls a story about a man who hates himself.

The guests ask whether the game is actually fun, saying critics praise its technical scope but that they nearly quit after thirty minutes. Boreing forced himself through four of eight planned hours and explains he dislikes the white lower class Miami thug aesthetic and the characters. He compares it to enjoying Scorsese films, where you watch rather than decide to kill a cop. Owen says the problem is pacing, since Red Dead Redemption 2 also had a barn building chore, but placed it three quarters through the game. Gibson says that making players spend six hours bored is bad game design and that the entertainment must come first, before any message. He ties it to games like Concord and Dragon Age.

Gibson says the industry once leaned left but with a balance of roughly sixty to forty, and many conservatives held leadership and key talent roles. He cites the original Halo's composer and voice director being pushed out of Bungie and Palmer Luckey leaving Oculus. He then tells his own story. After he tweeted that he was a pro-life game developer when the Supreme Court upheld the Texas heartbeat law, the tweet drew twelve million views and a wave of press coverage. He was told ninety percent of employees would quit unless he stepped down as CEO. After seventeen years building the company, he was locked out, though he owned forty-one percent.

Gibson says five to fifteen of 125 employees destroyed the company with a militant leftist agenda, and that the company has done poorly since. They sold at the peak of the market, and he believes God had him come back to make entertainment first games. His new company, Templar Media, is conservative and Judeo-Christian leaning, and has hired designers who worked on Call of Duty, Bungie titles, Red Dead and GTA. He is making a Bible-based open world adventure called Gate Zero. He says the world needs great Christian entertainment rather than bad Christian entertainment, and Owen praises the effort.

Owen says conservatives have long neglected the arts, letting leftists take over movies, TV, comics and games, while right-leaning people inside stay quiet. Boreing says two things that anger people online are telling them not to be anonymous and telling them they can succeed, because the spirit of the age sells despair and victimhood. He argues anonymity does not protect people from cancellation but enables it, since eighty million Trump voters cannot all be canceled. Conservatives should be predators rather than zebras. He relays a friend's view that conservatives claim to believe in the true, beautiful and good but only believe in the literal, and says young men should not be told to avoid games.

Boreing says he wants conservatives to make great movies, games, coffee and steak, and that a loser mentality and grifting hurt the cause. He argues people avoid agency because freedom is hard, and compares it to the Israelites wanting to return to Egypt. Gibson recalls a lawyer friend telling him that all fifteen of his games made a profit and urging him to return. Owen says he believes in white male privilege, defined as growing up with no one telling him he could not do things, and rejects online voices telling young men that women and the left are to blame. Boreing agrees that victim mentality is the worst poison, especially when real problems reinforce it.

Boreing says some young men ask why they cannot have their own culture as other groups do. He replies that black culture in America has been hollowed out by powerful people selling victimhood, and he names the Great Society as the real modern oppression, saying he does not want that sold to Gen Z. Owen says he is a quarter black and has seen defeatism in his family firsthand, including relatives who put his father down for going to college. Boreing says the thought I can will save a young man's life, though not his soul, and that if you do things, you will have done things.

Boreing argues that if young men believe they cannot succeed, they lose nothing by trying, and if he is right, the keys are waiting. Because peers believe they cannot, anyone who tries has a huge advantage, and even mediocre people with will could be princes. Owen and Gibson agree, noting that Owen's eighteen-year-old daughter is the manager's favorite for simply looking people in the eye, while the young men she meets show her TikToks. Boreing says Project Hail Mary felt like the America he grew up in. Gibson says he grew up poor in the rural Midwest, and that his mother told him he could do things and a great uncle made a grades bet with him.

Asked where the culture is hopeful, Gibson says the games industry is a success story for the culture war. Like new media, it has little barrier between creators, tools and audiences, since a film needs tens of millions of dollars while a game may need a few tens of thousands. He cites Queen's Domain, made by two people with a quarter of a million copies sold, and says players punish studios that preach, as with BioWare. Owen agrees that AAA studios are struggling while indie games thrive, citing Schedule One, a drug-dealing game made by one person. Major game engines and tools like Blender are free, though the work is still very hard.

Boreing says Lois Lane taking a helicopter in the 1970s Superman versus a newspaper having none in Batman v Superman shows how much less money media has. Games will see fewer billion dollar hits, but fortunes remain. He tells of a film school friend of his colleague Jonathan Hay who turned down helping on his 95,000 dollar Western because his first movie had to be Citizen Kane. He advises people to make the movie, game or book, because nobody is good at the start. Boreing says that he is proud of every film he made, including the weaker ones, because they led to the next.

Gibson says quality is lacking across entertainment, with Marvel movies failing and AAA games struggling, so creators can succeed while competition is weak. He says younger people are hungry for truth and open to the gospel, and his new game has 600,000 social media followers compared with 40,000 at his old company. He wants games that are undeniably great and that serve the underrepresented conservative majority, which he puts at over 60 percent of gamers. Owen cites data that most players choose the heroic path, including 92 percent in Mass Effect and only 15 percent trying the evil run in Baldur's Gate 3. He criticizes Rings of Power and says the era of the anti-hero is over.

Boreing says that for parents or wives worried about gaming, hobbies and escape are good, and not everything unproductive is bad, since rest is part of God's intention for people in Christianity and Judaism. In moderation gameplay can be very good. He says that the fact most players pick the good character shows what young men aspire to, and that picturing yourself as a hero is central to becoming one. Art imitates life, he says, and life imitates art. The guests recall the line that fairy tales teach that dragons can be slain, and Boreing ends by asking the most fun game to play with friends, then thanks them.
sg: Boring pacing and bad game design
John Gibson on being forced out
Victimhood, black culture and just trying
